newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: New Pakistan PM agrees to peace talks with India.
newsitem.headline: New Pakistan PM agrees to peace talks with India.

text.p: Pakistan's new Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif agreed on Thursday to resume stalled peace talks with arch-rival India to settle a dispute over Kashmir and other differences.

Sharif proposed that he and India Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda meet after preparatory talks by senior officials. In India a senior official said his government would respond "constructively" to Pakistan's offer.

Sharif said in a letter to the Indian prime minister, copies of which were released by the Pakistani Foreign Ministry, that foreign ministry secretaries of the two countries meet before the end of March to "prepare the ground for meaningful discussions" between the two prime ministers.

The letter responded to one sent by Deve Gowda on February 17 to congratulate Sharif on taking office and proposing a resumption of talks on a wide range of issues, including the disputed Himalayan region of Jammu and Kashmir.
The two countries have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947, two of them over Kashmir, two-thirds of which is ruled by India and the rest by Pakistan.
A senior Indian official in New Delhi said his government would respond "constructively" to Sharif's offer.
"India's response is already known. The prime minister has already said that we are ready to react to it constructively," the official told Reuters on condition of anonymity.

New Delhi regards the whole of Kashmir as an integral part of India. But Islamabad wants the predominantly Moslem Kashmiris to decide in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.

Sharif said in his letter that he was encouraged by Deve Gowda's willingness for wide-ranging and comprehensive talks on all issues of mutual concern, but added: "I hope you will agree with me that without some progress on the core issue of Jammu and Kashmir, it will be difficult to initiate meaningful cooperation in economic and cultural fields."

Bilateral talks between the two sides had broken down in January 1994 because of deep differences on Kashmir, where India is fighting a Moslem separatist revolt in the two-thirds of the region it controls.
Pakistan has insisted that Kashmir must be an essential part of any peace negotiations.

"I am deeply conscious of the need to free South Asia of tensions and conflicts so that our peoples can participate on equal terms in the global march towards progress and prosperity," Sharif said in his letter.
"For too long has South Asia remained mired in hostilities and conflicts, dissipating its precious resources," he said in a reference to the wars between the two countries and their military buildup.

He said he fully shared Deve Gowda's belief that as the two countries approached the 50th anniversary of their independence, there was an historic opportunity for their political leadership to deal with all outstanding disputes.
